newsitem.title: UK: EU work ruling could further sour ties with Britain.
newsitem.headline: EU work ruling could further sour ties with Britain.

text.p: A European Union directive limiting working hours appears unlikely to have much practical impact on British business, despite howls of protest from the Conservative government and senior industrialists.

Its most damaging effect could be in further souring relations between Britain and its 14 EU partners, many of whom are already weary of what they see as the UK's consistently jaundiced view of their efforts to achieve closer integration.

"It's a piece of legislation we would prefer not to have, but we can very comfortably work within it," said Niall FitzGerald, chairman of giant multinational Unilever Plc and of the Confederation of British Industry's Europe Committee.
He said British business was already suffering "from our waning influence in Europe because we're seen not to be constructively engaged with shaping Europe."

"I think if this leads to a further wave of anti-European rhetoric, then that will inevitably damage us further. That will not be in the interests of business and not in the interests of jobs in the United Kingdom," FitzGerald told Sky Television.
The European Court of Justice on Tuesday rejected Britain's challenge to a directive which says employees do not have to work an average of more than 48 hours per week unless they choose to.
Prime Minister John Major has threatened to block progress on European Union reforms unless the directive is reversed.

Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang said the directive could cost British industry up to 2.00 billion pounds ($3.31 billion) a year, but independent economists and EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn were sceptical about the figure.
Britons already have the longest working week in the EU, according to European Commission figures. They work an average of 43.4 hours per week while German workers average 39.9 and France's 39.7.

But few Britons work anything like 48 hours, says Lynne Imeson, director of policy at Nottinghamshire Chamber of Commerce. A survey of its member firms in 1995 showed only nine percent of them had working hours in excess of 42 hours a week.
"There is a cost as far as health and safety measures are concerned but there is also a benefit," Flynn told the BBC.

Dan Corry, senior economist at the Institute of Public Policy Research, a left-wing think-tank, doubts that the ruling will have much effect on business and noted that its introduction was not a major issue in other EU countries.
"This particular measure is not one that European employers rail about, although they do rail about other things such as restrictions on their ability to fire people," Corry said.
"I would be very surprised if in five years' time anyone can pick up any effect on anything from this measure."
Corry said the negative reaction from British companies to the court ruling might reflect the fact that they had got used to 17 years of deregulation under a Conservative government.

"I think what is worrying business is more the symbolic idea that they have had a government which has been taking any restrictions away from management so management can decide everything as they want," he said.
"They are now asking if this is a turning back towards a social democracy or Christian democracy type of world."
Some of the comments from Conservative politicians suggested that it was indeed the symbolic rather than the practical significance of the directive that concerned them most.
"It is burdensome to employers," said David Howell, Conservative chairman of the House of Commons Foreign Affairs Select Committee.

"Also it is a very sinister precedent for the future, pushing through social and detailed legislation, much better negotiated near the workplace by the nation state, on the basis of an article in the Treaty that shouldn't really cover these things."
Andrew Buxton, chairman of Barclays Bank, took a similar view.

"The point about this legislation is not that the 48-hour week will be a disaster for British industry," he said. "The real point is that it signifies creeping European legislation introducing regulations to the British labour market." ($1=.6050 Pound)
